[There's never been a better time to go into math](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LKrwhjOI8Nc),
3Blue1Brown, 16 October 2026, 41 minutes.

Grant Sanderson talks on his own, without a guest, about where mathematics goes
once AI can do research-level work. The video works through three kinds of
machine in turn: a proof machine, a conjecture machine and a theory machine.
It then asks what is left if AI is better at all of them, and closes on why now
is a good time to start in mathematics.

**Even if AI gets very good at proofs, there are large opportunities in theory
building.** That is the idea I liked most.

**The same holds in my own modelling work.** I am already thinking about
theories for the T-cell engager (TCE) models and the pharmacokinetic (PK) and
B-cell models: understanding these models better, such as the sources of
variability in how parameters affect response.

Terence Tao makes a related argument in
[Mathematics in the age of AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16753), that a
result is not part of mathematics until people understand it. The
[post on publishing explanations](../../blog/posts/2026-10-15-explaining-the-work-as-part-of-publishing/index.qmd)
carries that argument over to pharmacometrics.
